extracted.intended_audience: readers of the Public Advertiser; politically engaged English public and parliamentarians (18th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles embedded in an 18th-century series of political letters (Junius) aimed at criticizing government conduct and instructing public/political debate. Focuses on rhetorical conduct, public virtue, parliamentary privilege, and foreign/domestic policy judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indulging first emotions of resentment before publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware how you indulge the first emotions of your resentment. This paper is delivered to the world, and cannot be recalled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication is irreversible: the prosecution of an innocent printer cannot alter facts or refute arguments. Do not furnish your opponents with further materials against yourself by reacting too hastily or vindictively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to understanding and conscience, not force
rubrics_metrics.description: An honest man, like the true religion, appeals to the understanding, or modestly confides in the eternal evidence of his conscience. The impostor employs force instead of argument, imposes silence where he cannot convince, and propagates his character by the sword.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good persuasion uses reason and moral evidence. Anti-pattern: using coercion, legal force, or intimidation to suppress opponents or public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not provide opponents with self-incriminating material
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not furnish me with farther materials against yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accused or criticized, refrain from actions or words that supply additional, durable evidence of wrongdoing. Tactical restraint preserves one's position and avoids strengthening the critic's case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public declarations should preserve apparent veracity
rubrics_metrics.description: When the first magistrate speaks to the nation, some care should be taken of his apparent veracity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders' speeches must be credible and consistent with facts and subsequent actions. Empty or equivocal phrasing (a 'guard and reserve in the choice of expression') undermines public trust and prepares the ground for dishonourable compromises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cunning and secret management are dishonorable in public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: In public affairs, cunning, let it be ever so well wrought, will not conduct a man honourably through life. Like bad money, it may be current for a time, but it will soon be cried down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open, generous conduct befits public office. Secret systems of the closet and private intrigues that control the sovereign without avowal are condemned as cowardly and corrupt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers should act openly and take responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of acting that open, generous part which becomes your rank and station, you meanly skulk into the closet, and give your sovereign such advice as you have not the spirit to avow or defend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials ought to avow and defend their advice publicly rather than manipulate power anonymously. Anti-pattern: exercising power while declining titles/official responsibility to enjoy emoluments without accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sacrifice national honour or public interest for secret diplomatic schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan of domestic policy which has been invariably pursued ... engrosses all the attention of his servants. Rather than suffer the execution of that scheme to be delayed or interrupted, the king has been advised to make a public surrender ... of the interests of his subjects, and of his own personal reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign policy and negotiations must not be allowed to produce secret accommodations that compromise public rights or national dignity. Evaluate diplomacy by its effects on public honour and the people's rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish restitution from reparation; principle matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Restitution of a possession, and reparation of an injury, are as different in substance as they are in language. The very act of restitution may contain ... a shameful aggravation of the injury. A man of spirit does not measure the degree of an injury by the mere positive damage he has sustained; he considers the principle on which it is founded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging settlements, assess whether the opponent's asserted rights/principles are being conceded. A nominal restitution that preserves an enemy's claim can be worse than refusing restitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate peace vs war by security of peace and lost opportunity for advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Between peace and war abstractedly ... The real questions are, 'Have we any security that the peace we have so dearly purchased will last a twelvemonth?' and, if not, 'Have we, or have we not, sacrificed the fairest opportunity of making war with advantage?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions for peace should consider the durability of the peace and whether a strategic opportunity for advantageous war has been needlessly surrendered. Beware abstract declamations that ignore concrete circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary privilege should be strictly ascertained and narrowly confined
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essentially necessary to the preservation of the constitution, that the privileges of parliament should be strictly ascertained, and confined within the narrowest bounds the nature of the institution will admit of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privileges without definition become instruments of arbitrary power. The degree of submission to privilege is a question of convenience, proportioned to the confidence reposed in representatives; unchecked privilege risks being used under the direction of the crown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to privilege is justified when representatives betray public trust
rubrics_metrics.description: We trusted our representatives with privileges for their own defence and ours. We cannot hinder their desertion, but we can prevent their carrying over their arms to the service of the enemy. ... It is indifferent to me whether the crown ... imposes new laws, or whether the same arbitrary power produces the same effects through the medium of the house of commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the house of commons acts as agent of undue influence or crown-directed interests, limiting or resisting its privileges may be necessary to protect legal liberty and public interest. Historical/contextual caution: changes of circumstance can alter the rightful degree of deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers should maintain independence from court patronage and preserve reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: To write for profit, without taxing the press; to write for fame, and to be unknown; to support the intrigues of faction, and to be disowned as a dangerous auxiliary by every party in the kingdom, are contradictions which the minister must reconcile before I forfeit my credit with the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A political writer's reputation and independence are pledges of attachment to the people. Selling out to court favour undermines credibility; maintaining an honourable reputation may require refusing office or patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise language to avoid equivocation and prepare public for honourable conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The excessive caution with which the speech was drawn up, had impressed upon me an early conviction, that no serious resentment was thought of, and that the conclusion of the business ... must, in some degree, be dishonourable to England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evasive or equivocal phrasing by governments signals unwillingness to act decisively; evaluate such language skeptically. Precision in official language preserves appearance and substance of honour.
